analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act unless at least 7 million people enrolled through its insurance exchanges.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to eight House committees and its health subcommittee in December 2013, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The NUMBER Act would have automatically repealed the Affordable Care Act — its subsidies, its Medicaid expansion, and its insurance rules — if the Comptroller General did not certify that at least 7 million people had signed up for health plans through the law's exchanges by March 31, 2014. The bill was referred to eight House committees the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, so it had no effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Had it passed, the main beneficiaries would have been higher-income households and stakeholders who opposed the Affordable Care Act's taxes and rules, since repeal would have ended the law's coverage expansion while restoring the pre-2010 insurance rules that let insurers deny coverage or charge more to people with pre-existing conditions. Millions of enrollees would have lost subsidized coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Opponents of the health law's taxes and rules

how_it_helps.text: For people who opposed the Affordable Care Act on constitutional or fiscal grounds, the bill offered an automatic repeal if the law's early enrollment fell short of 7 million people, removing the need for a separate repeal vote.

analysis.who_pays: Had it passed, the cost would have fallen on the millions of low- and moderate-income people who gained coverage through the exchanges and the Medicaid expansion, and on people with pre-existing conditions who would have returned to an insurance market that could deny or price them out.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on ACA coverage subsidies

drawbacks.text: The bill would have repealed the ACA outright — ending subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and protections for people with pre-existing conditions — based on a single enrollment number rather than on any assessment of whether the law was working for the people enrolled in it.

The 7-million enrollment target was set before the troubled rollout of Healthcare.gov; actual enrollment in the first open enrollment period ultimately reached about 8 million, so a rigid statutory trigger tied to a rolling tally of sign-ups was a fragile basis for repealing an entire law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Had it become law, the bill would have removed subsidized health coverage from millions of people if enrollment fell short of an arbitrary target — a large cost with little offsetting benefit beyond the bill's stated constitutional objection to the individual mandate. In practice, the repeal never advanced, so its drawbacks never materialized; the main effect of what actually happened is that nothing changed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to eight House committees and one of their subcommittees, and no committee or chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 16, 2013 and referred to eight committees, including Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and the Rules Committee.
On December 20, 2013 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on December 27 to the Subcommittee on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs.
No committee approved the bill, no floor vote was held, and no further action appears in the record before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on Affordable Care Act subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and protections for pre-existing conditions kept that coverage, since the repeal never advanced. Opponents of the health law lost a vehicle for ending it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People keeping ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. Ted Yoho
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set its repeal-if-enrollment-lags structure.

for.name: 25 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 25 cosponsors were Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill received no Democratic support in the record; it also never advanced to any vote.

industries.note: Repeal would have eliminated the exchange marketplaces where insurers sell subsidized plans to millions of customers, shrinking that business. Some insurers might have welcomed the end of ACA rules, but the largest effect was loss of the new guaranteed subsidized market.
Hospitals had accepted lower payments in exchange for the coverage expansion; losing the Medicaid expansion and subsidies would have shifted costs back to emergency care for the uninsured.

industries.industry: Low- and moderate-income households without employer coverage
industries.note: The people the bill treated as a benchmark — exchange enrollees — were the ones who would have lost subsidized coverage if enrollment fell short of the target.
